newsitem.title: USA: U.S. renews willingness to mull new N. Korea aid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. renews willingness to mull new N. Korea aid.

text.p: With North Korea stalling on peace talks, the United States on Monday played down talk of war on the Korean peninsula and reaffirmed willingness to consider more food aid for Pyongyang, but not as part of a deal to launch the negotiations.

For the fourth day in a row chief U.S. negotiator Charles Kartman and his South Korean counterpart were ready to enter into senior-level talks with a North Korean delegation, but it seemed unlikely that the meeting -- adjourned from last Wednesday -- would take place on Monday.

The aim was to hear North Korea's reply to a year-old United States-South Korean proposal for four-party peace talks that would finally close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War and replace a fraying armistice with a peace treaty.

Although North Korea negotiators told American and South Korean counterparts last week they essentially accepted the proposal, they conditioned that acceptance on demands for more food aid and lifting U.S. trade sanctions, officials said.

"At this point ... the North Koreans seem reluctant to come back to the Republic of Korea and the United States for the kind of full working session that we had anticipated," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
He told reporters the peace talks proposal remains on the table but whether Pyongyang will accept it "is anyone's guess. And so there is a bit of a muddle in New York right now, a diplomatic muddle."

A high-level North Korean defector, Hwang Jang-yop, who arrived in Seoul Monday, raised alarms by reporting that North Koreans "have lost hope" and their desperate Stalinist government seems intent on waging war.

Burns said while the border between North and South is one of the most dangerous spots on Earth, the United States, with 37,000 troops there, remains ready to defend South Korea if needed and will maintain its military presence. But he noted that the landmark 1994 U.S.-North Korean accord freezing Pyongyang's nuclear programme was working well.

So despite Hwang's comments "we think that actually the events seem to indicate that the North Koreans, at least, are open to further talk with the United States, with South Korea, with Japan, with other countries in Asia who are interested in peace and security on the Korean Peninsula," he said.

Kartman, acting assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific Affairs, returned to Washington on Saturday but was ready to fly back to New York -- venue for the talks -- when North Korea is ready to meet, Burns said.
There may be "working level" contacts on Monday, as there had been over the weekend. The U.S. side is willing to remain on hold in New York a while longer but not forever, Burns said.

On the food aid issue, Burns reiterated earlier comments that "If the (U.N.) World Food Programme comes forward again and says: 'It's not enough from the international comunity. We need more. We would obviously look at that very seriously."

The United States already responded twice this year to WFP food appeals for North Korea, contributing $25 million. It has "shown its good faith on this issue (and the already promised aid) may not be the end of the story," Burns said.

"We just hope to assure them that food aid is coming ... through the United Nations and through private voluntary organisations, and that they ought to be assured that we have made a good-faith proposal in the four-party talks," he said.

But North Korea, on the verge of famine, needs far more food than pledged so far. South Korea and Japan have been holding back, waiting to see if the peace talks are launched. Also, Pyongyang's ability to enter into commercial deals is hampered by U.S. trade sanctions.
U.S. officials have said all this is open for discussion once peace talks begin. But Pyongang "wants the issues to be joined," Burns said.

For now, he said, "We don't believe the food aid should be a precondition or a condition or linked in any way to these talks." As for lifting trade sanctions, "the United States is not in a position to take any further action until we see where we're going in this relationship. And the sanctions remain in place, and with good reason."
